issues.legal_issue: Dispensing with the statutory objection inquiry in a land acquisition requires a genuine urgency supported by relevant material, and planned development alone does not establish that urgency.
material_facts: The acquisition was for planned industrial development over a large area, but the authorities did not identify a specific urgency that required omitting the opportunity to object.
A prior acquisition from the same village for the same purpose had proceeded with an objection inquiry.
More than a year passed between the development authority’s request for urgent acquisition and the acquisition notification, without an explanation for the delay.
The stated risk of encroachment was the only identified ground for urgency and did not explain why an objection inquiry had to be dispensed with.
There was also an unexplained delay of about a year between the acquisition notification and the declaration notification.
issues.conclusion: The State had no relevant material supporting genuine subjective satisfaction that the objection inquiry had to be dispensed with; invoking the urgency power for that purpose was unjustified.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 4, 5-A, 6 and 17(1) and (4) of the Land Acquisition Act, read with the Uttar Pradesh amendments, make the objection inquiry the normal procedure and permit its omission only when a genuine urgency, supported by relevant material, warrants it. A court may examine whether relevant material existed, though it does not reappraise a properly supported subjective satisfaction as an appellate authority. Planned development does not automatically justify dispensing with the inquiry. The Court applied Narayan Govind Gavate v. State of Maharashtra, which requires attention to whether urgency warrants eliminating the inquiry; State of U.P. v. Pista Devi and A.P. Sareen v. State of U.P., which recognize that urgency may arise in appropriate development cases but do not establish an automatic rule; Rajasthan Housing Board v. Shri Kisan, where concrete time-bound circumstances supported urgency; and Gurdial Singh v. State of Punjab, concerning the importance of the inquiry and the need for real urgency.

rule.if: land_acquisition_challenge and specific_urgency_material_absent and (encroachment_only_basis or unexplained_acquisition_delay)

predicates.land_acquisition_challenge: The proceeding challenges an acquisition of land for a public purpose.
predicates.specific_urgency_material_absent: The acquiring authority did not have material showing why the circumstances required the ordinary objection process to be omitted.
predicates.encroachment_only_basis: The authority relied on the possibility of encroachment as its stated reason for omitting the objection process.
predicates.unexplained_acquisition_delay: A substantial delay in acting on the acquisition request or completing the acquisition steps was left unexplained.

issues.definition: When a land acquisition challenge shows that specific urgency material was absent and the authority relied on possible encroachment or left substantial acquisition delays unexplained, the objection inquiry cannot justifiably be dispensed with.

issues.legal_issue: Whether acquired land qualifies as protected abadi land under a government policy is a disputed factual matter that cannot be conclusively determined on the record of this proceeding.
material_facts: The appellants claimed that their lands had existing residential or industrial construction and were covered by a policy against acquiring abadi land.

The evidence about the nature, extent and timing of the construction was disputed; the record included a civil-court finding in one case, a pending further appeal, and conflicting inspection material.
The State was not a party to the civil-court proceedings, and the evidence did not establish whether the lands were village-site lands or whether the construction existed at the relevant time.
The appellants accepted that the Court need not decide the abadi issue if they could pursue a suitable alternative remedy.
issues.conclusion: The Court made no finding that the lands were protected abadi land or immune from acquisition; it left the question open for consideration by the State authorities on the appellants’ representations.
issues.legal_principle: A court deciding a writ challenge cannot determine a claimed exemption where material factual questions remain disputed, including the character and timing of construction and whether a government policy covers it. A prior civil-court finding does not bind a State that was not a party to that proceeding. The Court left the matter for the State authorities to assess, including whether abadi existed at the relevant time, was legally permissible, continued to exist, and came within a policy then in force. The judgment discusses the proposed representation under Section 48(1) of the Land Acquisition Act as the route for that consideration.

predicates.land_acquisition_writ: The proceeding is a writ challenge to a land acquisition.
predicates.abadi_status_disputed: The parties dispute whether the acquired land had qualifying residential settlement or construction at the relevant time.
predicates.abadi_policy_coverage_unresolved: The record does not establish whether a policy against acquiring such land applied to the land.

issues.definition: In a land acquisition writ, disputed abadi status and unresolved policy coverage leave the claimed exemption for determination by the appropriate authority rather than the court.

issues.legal_issue: A court exercising discretionary appellate jurisdiction may decline to set aside an acquisition despite an unjustified omission of the objection inquiry when the circumstances make that relief impracticable and a suitable alternative remedy remains available.
material_facts: The acquisition covered about 494 acres, while the appellants’ dispute concerned about 50 acres; most of the acquired land was not under challenge.
Development work and infrastructure had proceeded on the undisputed land, and setting aside the acquisition for the appellants’ parcels risked disrupting the wider project.
The challenge had remained pending for more than six years.
The appellants did not challenge the public purpose or allege mala fides.
The appellants’ principal remaining grievance, concerning abadi land, could be presented to the State authorities through a representation.
issues.conclusion: The Court declined to interfere under Article 136 or set aside the acquisition notifications, notwithstanding its conclusion that dispensing with the objection inquiry was unjustified; it dismissed the appeals subject to liberty to make representations.
issues.legal_principle: The Supreme Court’s jurisdiction under Article 136 is discretionary and is exercised in light of the circumstances of the case. The Court may refuse to set aside an acquisition where most of a large project is uncontested, development has proceeded, only a smaller portion is challenged after substantial delay, the public purpose and good faith are not disputed, and the principal grievance can be pursued through an alternative remedy. The Court relied on Article 136 and the circumstances of the acquisition and proceedings; it did not treat the defect in dispensing with the inquiry as requiring automatic relief.

rule.if: land_acquisition_appeal and (most_acquired_land_uncontested and project_development_advanced) and challenge_delayed and alternative_remedy_available and no_public_purpose_or_mala_fides_challenge

predicates.land_acquisition_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a land acquisition.
predicates.most_acquired_land_uncontested: Most of the land covered by the acquisition is not challenged by the appellants.
predicates.project_development_advanced: Development or infrastructure work has proceeded on the uncontested land.
predicates.challenge_delayed: The challenge has remained pending for a substantial period before the court is asked to grant relief.
predicates.alternative_remedy_available: The appellants can present their principal remaining grievance to an appropriate authority through another available process.
predicates.no_public_purpose_or_mala_fides_challeng: The appellants do not contest the public purpose or allege that the acquisition was made in bad faith.

issues.definition: When a delayed land-acquisition appeal concerns only a portion of an otherwise uncontested and substantially developed project, leaves public purpose and good faith unchallenged, and has an alternative remedy available, the court may decline to set aside the acquisition.

issues.legal_issue: Where the acquired land remains in the owners’ possession, they may ask the State to consider withdrawing it from acquisition, but the State must determine whether the claimed abadi and applicable policy justify release.
material_facts: The authorities relied on a possession certificate covering numerous parcels, but no possession receipt signed by the appellants was produced.
The certificate appeared to record paper possession, while evidence showed that some disputed parcels remained occupied and had construction or an operating factory.
A court order requiring the status quo to be maintained followed the asserted taking of possession, and the Court concluded that actual possession of the appellants’ lands had not been taken.
The appellants’ proposed ground for release was that their lands had qualifying abadi covered by the State’s policy.
issues.conclusion: The Court permitted the appellants to make representations seeking withdrawal of their lands from acquisition and directed the State to consider timely representations, while expressing no view on whether the lands should be released.
issues.legal_principle: Section 48(1) of the Land Acquisition Act permits the Government to withdraw from an acquisition of land of which possession has not been taken. The Court found that the evidence did not establish actual possession of the appellants’ lands and allowed the State to consider representations on whether qualifying abadi and an applicable government policy warranted withdrawal. It required the State to hear the appellants and decide the matter, but did not direct release or prejudge the merits.

predicates.land_acquisition_dispute: The proceeding concerns land that has been acquired by the State.
predicates.actual_possession_not_taken: The State has not in fact taken possession of the land, even if a document records an asserted or paper transfer of possession.
predicates.timely_release_representation_filed: The landowners file a representation within the time allowed by the court or applicable process, asking the State to withdraw the land from acquisition.

issues.definition: When actual possession has not been taken and the landowners timely seek withdrawal, the State must consider their representation but is not thereby required to release the land.

issues.legal_issue: An intervener who did not bring the original writ proceeding may be allowed to pursue an independent writ petition where the intervener’s separate factual grievances were not examined in the appeal.
material_facts: An intervener alleged that land had been acquired for allocation to persons connected with public officials and raised other serious objections involving disputed facts.
The intervener had not filed a writ petition in the High Court whose judgment was under appeal.
The respondents did not oppose allowing the intervener to pursue a separate writ petition.
issues.conclusion: The Court allowed the intervener to file a substantive writ petition in the High Court and left the merits and maintainability of that petition for the High Court to decide.
issues.legal_principle: An intervener’s independent grievance, particularly one involving disputed facts and not raised in the original writ proceeding, need not be determined in an appeal concerning other petitioners. The intervener may pursue a substantive proceeding under Article 226, with the High Court deciding its merits and maintainability after hearing the parties. The Court expressed no opinion on either.

predicates.appeal_from_other_landowners_writ: The appeal arises from a writ proceeding brought by landowners other than the intervener.
predicates.intervener_has_independent_disputed_grie: The intervener raises a separate grievance involving facts not determined in the appeal.
predicates.intervener_did_not_file_original_writ: The intervener was not an original petitioner in the writ proceeding under appeal.

issues.definition: When an appeal concerns other landowners and an intervener has a separate disputed grievance but did not file the original writ, the intervener may bring an independent writ for the High Court to decide.
